# The gate

The gate runs the seven steps below on one tree, in about 25 minutes. It is green if every step passes, and red if one fails. If a step fails, run the rest, so that the summary holds every step's result.

## What it writes

The summary, `summary.txt`, has one tab-separated row for each suite: `track/suite`, tests, failures, errors, skipped. Below the rows, lines that start with `#` give each log's `BUILD` and `Total time:` lines, the machine that ran the gate (`# machine`), the atomic runs and the ladder's comparison. A landed summary can also end with `# microgpt-walk` lines: the `VERDICT:` and `rc=` lines of the microGPT walk check (`interpreter.md`, "The model program"), run on the landed tree. Add them only if your brief asks for the microGPT walk check on the landed tree.

If your brief asks you to land a gate's results, put them in a new `gate/` folder in `explorations/compile-ladder/`, under the `climb-batch-` name that your brief gives, in the form of the newest one: `summary.txt`, and in `ladder/` the files `ladder.tsv`, `microgpt-phase.md`, `comparison.txt` and `microgpt-comparison.txt`. The next gate compares with the newest summary there or in `explorations/compile-ladder/gate-baseline/`, and finds no other. Land them in a commit that changes nothing else that the gate reads.

Steps 5 and 7 use shell functions that `explorations/coordinator/tools/gate-functions.sh` defines. The file runs nothing. In each Bash call of steps 5 and 7, set up the call as `build-and-caches.md` says, which sets `FORTRESS_HOME` to the tree's root. Then source the file, from the root:

    source explorations/coordinator/tools/gate-functions.sh

## When to run it

Your brief says whether you run the gate. If it does not ask, run only your own tests (`tests-running.md`).

If it asks, first check whether the newest gate still holds for your tree. A gate's tables stay valid until the tree changes under `ProjectFortress/` or `Library/`, or in `build.xml`, outside the test files. A test file is a `.fss`, `.fsi` or `.test` file directly in `ProjectFortress/tests/` or a `ProjectFortress/*_tests/` directory. The commit that landed the newest summary changed nothing that the gate reads. Commit your tree, then run this command. It prints each path, test files excepted, changed since that commit:

    G=$(git log -1 --format=%H -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt')
    git diff --name-only $G HEAD -- ProjectFortress Library build.xml \
        | grep -v -E '^ProjectFortress/([^/]*_)?tests/[^/]*\.(fss|fsi|test)$'

- If it prints a path, run the gate.
- If not, the newest gate holds. Run only the changed test files, through `harness-one.sh` and `junit.sh` (`tests-running.md`).

## The steps

Run these steps from the tree's root. Keep the logs of steps 2 and 4 in `tmp/gate/`, as `compileAll.txt`, `testFast.txt`, `testSystem.txt` and `testSpecData.txt`.

1. Read the Avail column of `df -h /`. Warning: deleting `/tmp/fortress*rats` can break other live runs. If the column shows less than 1 GB, delete `/tmp/fortress*rats`, `ProjectFortress/test-tmp` and `ProjectFortress/test-caches`, and read it again. If it still shows less than 500 MB, stop and report.
2. Run `rm -rf ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS tmp/gate && mkdir -p tmp/gate`, then `ant compileAll`.
3. If the build printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, run the library order (`build-and-caches.md`). If not, and a source of the compiler's library changed since the caches were filled, take its step in `build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library". Then copy the caches twice for the ladder regression, before anything else compiles into them:

       D=$PWD/tmp/gate/ladder ; mkdir -p $D/root
       cp -a default_repository/caches $D/root/ladder-caches
       cp -a default_repository/caches $D/root/pristine

4. Run `ant testFast`, then `ant testSystem`, then `ant testSpecData`. All three must have zero failures. In `ant testSystem`, `tests/XXXAtomicNestedReadsKeptWalk` can print `PASS` and fail with 'Missing expected failure': its expected failure depends on a race (ledger row 1004). The gate is then red, as for any failure. Cite the row in your report.
5. Write the summary: `gate_summary tmp/gate tmp/gate/summary.txt`. Compare it: `gate_compare "$(last_landed_summary)" tmp/gate/summary.txt`. It prints a line for a suite with failures or errors, a suite with no tests, a suite whose count of tests fell, and a suite that is gone. Each such line makes the gate red. A count that rose prints nothing.
6. Do the atomic runs, and append their lines to the summary.
7. Do the ladder regression.

## The atomic runs

The atomic runs compile the programs below, and run each one three times at four threads. They need the library's jars in the tree's caches (`build-and-caches.md`). Run them from `ProjectFortress/`:

    for p in AtomicTopLevelObjectVar AtomicTopLevelVar MutableTopLevelVarInLoop FirstLoadThreadsRungG \
             AlsoArmThrowsJoinsCompiled CallArgumentsForkCompiled AtomicOwnWriteNestedCompiled \
             AtomicNestedSameBodyCompiled NestedAtomicAbortCompiled AtomicNestedViewCompiled \
             AtomicSharedReadsCompiled AtomicThrowRevertsCompiled AtomicExprCompiled AtomicFieldCompiled \
             atomic0 atomic1 atomic2 atomic3 atomic4 atomic5 atomic6 \
             nestedTransactions0 nestedTransactions1 nestedTransactions2 ; do
      d=other_compiler_tests ; [ -f compiler_tests/$p.fss ] && d=compiler_tests
      timeout -k 5 300 ../bin/fortress compile $d/$p.fss >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "# atomic $p COMPILE-FAILED" ; continue ; }
      for i in 1 2 3 ; do
        out=$(FORTRESS_THREADS=4 timeout -k 5 120 ../bin/fortress run $p 2>&1) ; rc=$?
        [ $rc -eq 124 ] && { out=$(FORTRESS_THREADS=4 timeout -k 5 120 ../bin/fortress run $p 2>&1) ; rc=$? ; }
        case "$out" in *FAIL*) r=FAIL ;; *PASS*) r=PASS ;; *) r="NO-PASS rc=$rc" ;; esac
        [ $rc -eq 124 ] && r=TIMEOUT-TWICE
        echo "# atomic $p run$i threads=4 $r"
      done
    done

The gate is red on any FAIL, NO-PASS, COMPILE-FAILED or TIMEOUT-TWICE.

## The ladder regression

The compile ladder records how far each test program gets through the compiler's phases, in order: parse, disambiguate, typecheck, codegen, link, run and pass. The ladder regression runs part of it again, and compares the result with the baseline, `explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/`:

- It compiles and runs the 85 programs of the baseline's `pass-list.txt`. It compares each one's phase and output with the baseline's `raw/`.
- It compiles the eighteen components of the two microGPT programs, and never runs them. It compares each one's phase with the baseline's `microgpt-phase.md`.

A file that moved gets a mark:

- DOWN: a phase lower than the record.
- MISSING: a file with no output.
- STDOUT: output that differs from the record after the `Operation took <n>ms` line is masked.
- UP: a phase higher than the record. This is progress, not red.

DOWN, MISSING and STDOUT are red, unless your brief declared that move as expected before the gate ran.
Warning: do not run `run-ladder.sh`, the driver over every test program, with its defaults. Its default root is shared, its cache pruning corrupts a parallel run, and its default `OUT` is a tracked folder.

To run it, as step 7, with step 3's copies of the caches:

1. Copy the drivers into `tmp/gate/ladder/`, and point their outputs and caches there:

       D=$PWD/tmp/gate/ladder ; B=explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19
       cp explorations/compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static/run-subset.sh \
          $B/classify.py $B/microgpt-phase.sh $B/microgpt-phase.py $D/
       sed -i -e "s|^OUT=.*|OUT=$D|" -e "s|^LADDER_ROOT=.*|LADDER_ROOT=$D/root|" $D/run-subset.sh
       sed -i -e "s|/home/user/fortress|$PWD|g" \
           -e "s|^export LADDER_CACHES=.*|export LADDER_CACHES=$D/root/ladder-caches|" \
           -e "s|^export LADDER_TMP=.*|export LADDER_TMP=$D/root/ladder-tmp|" \
           -e "s|^RAW=.*|RAW=$D/raw/microgpt|" -e "s|^TSV=.*|TSV=$D/microgpt-results.tsv|" $D/microgpt-phase.sh
       tail -n +2 $B/pass-list.txt | cut -f1 | sed 's|/|\t|' > $D/subset.txt

2. Run the four scripts, with no arguments, in this order: `bash $D/run-subset.sh`, `python3 $D/classify.py`, `bash $D/microgpt-phase.sh` and `python3 $D/microgpt-phase.py`. Each reads and writes in `$D`. This takes about 200 s for the 85 and 35 s for the eighteen, so run them in the background (`session.md`, "Long commands"). With step 3's copies, the driver skips the library's build (about 145 s).
3. Compare: `ladder_compare $B $D`, then `diff <(mg_phases $B/microgpt-phase.md) <(mg_phases $D/microgpt-phase.md)`. Append each line that they print to the summary, with `# ladder ` before it.

If your brief asks for your change's own ladder subset, write your own `subset.txt`. Put in it each file whose recorded first error in the baseline's `raw/` names something that your change touched. Run them after your edit only. Compare them with the newest landed `ladder.tsv`, or with the baseline's `raw/` for a file that the gate does not run.

## Comparing with an earlier run

- `ant testSystem` runs in four shards, the summary's rows `system-0` to `system-3`. A shard takes the files by their place in a sorted list, so an added file moves every later file to another shard. When you compare by hand, compare only the sum of the four. `gate_compare` sums them.
- In printed output, mask only these differences: the `Operation took <n>ms` line, a Java line number in a stack frame, an object's identity hash (`@` and hex digits), and a position in a library file that your change moved. In your report, list each test with a masked difference, and the kinds masked in it.
- If your brief asks you to compare the interpreter tests with a base run, use the two scripts in `explorations/coordinator/tools/count-run/`. `count-run.sh` runs every `ProjectFortress/tests/*.fss` under walk, one JVM per test: run it once on the base commit and once after your edit. `compare-normalised.py` compares the two runs, with the last three masks above. Each script's header gives its usage.

# The library

The library is `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, without the compiler's own files there:

- In `Library/`: the interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi`, and its other components. The compiler's `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerAlgebra` and `CompilerSystem` are not part of it. `FortressAst.fss` and `.fsi` are generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`: edit that file, never these two.
- In `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: `FortressBuiltin`, `NativeArray` and the rest. The compiler's `CompilerBuiltin` is not part of it.
- `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, the top type, belongs to both libraries. After an edit to it, also take the compiled path's step (`build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library").
- `Library/incomplete/` is not on the source path (`default_repository/configuration`), so no program can import what it declares. Nothing that the suites or the model program run imports `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` either. Before you cite a declaration as the library's way, check that a running program can reach it.

## How loops and reductions call the library

The desugarer, which both paths share, turns these forms into calls of the library:

- `for x <- g do b end` becomes `g.loop(fn x => b)`, a call of the generator's `loop` method. Each further generator nests one more `loop` call inside.
- `while x <- e do b end` becomes `while __whileCond(e, fn x => b) do end`. `if x <- e then ... end` becomes a call of `__cond`.
- A comprehension or a big operator, such as `SUM`, becomes a call of `__bigOperator`, whose argument calls `__generate` on each generator. So does a big operator inside another: no desugaring calls the library's `__bigOperator2`.

These functions work on the library's generators and reductions: `trait Generator` and `trait Reduction` in `FortressLibrary.fsi`, and `RangeInternals.fss` for ranges. `FortressLibrary.fss` also defines `__loop`, but no desugaring calls it. So a failure inside a loop or a reduction is most often in the library's code, and its fix is a library edit.

## The curator's decisions on the library

- Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only. A range over another integer type is a static error, and walk stops when it builds one. Write a wider counter as a `ZZ32` loop that widens its index.
- `ZZ32` and numerals convert into `RR64` implicitly. `ZZ64` converts into `RR64` only explicitly, by `asFloat`.
- For arithmetic that wraps on overflow, use the wrapping operators ∔ `DOTPLUS`, ∸ `DOTMINUS` and ⨰ `DOTTIMES`. Parenthesise every such expression fully, because their precedence is stated only among themselves.
- `SUM` and `PROD` are generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`. The element type is written before the generators, as in `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. In the library, write it, as its own sites do. For a call without it, the checker takes the reduction's expected type, or else its body's type (`revival-changes.md`, "Reductions and comprehensions"). Walk runs such a call at its value's declared type, or else at the join of its elements' run-time types. An empty `SUM` with no static argument written and no declared type gives the integer 0, and an empty `PROD` the integer 1, whatever the body's type (ledger row 716). With a static argument written that is not a number type, such as a user group, an empty or filtered `SUM` ends in `CastError` (ledger row 436).
- An indexed type's index parameter is bounded by `Index` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). `BoundedRange[\I\]` cannot take the bound, because the open range `(:)` stays a range over `Any` (P-56). So its `atMost(n: I): FullRange[\I\]` has the condition `where { I extends Index }`, which each call must meet (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`). A type whose static parameter is a range's index type takes the bound too, as `UniformDistribution[\T extends Index\]` over a `FullRange[\T\]` (`Library/Random.fsi`).
- An array's `fill` takes a value, and its `tabulate` a function of the index: `array[\ZZ32\](4).fill(0)`, `array[\ZZ32\](4).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 10 i)`. The factories that take a function are `tabulatedArray1` to `tabulatedArray3` and `tabulatedVector`.

## Designing a change

- Put into this library a general declaration that a program had to write for itself. The plainest case is an operation that the library has for one number type, array rank or sibling trait and lacks for another. A declaration of the program's own domain stays in the program. Move a declaration out of the model program only if your brief asks: the move changes model lines.
- Fix a gap in the library, not by a workaround in the program that meets it. Take the design from the library's practice as well as from the specification's text. If the two disagree, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
- If a rule of the language or the checker refuses the way that you want, find how the library writes that kind of thing, and do the same. The checker's refusals of this library reach you through your brief, or through a run of the count stage (`compiler.md`): by default, `fortress typecheck` checks against the compiler's prelude.
- When you add a method, make it dotted or functional as its family in the library does. If the family shows no practice, follow the team's unfinished collection design (`Library/incomplete/Collection.fss`): an updater, a getter or a setter, indexing included, is dotted, and every other method is functional.
- A new functional method reserves its name: the phase that binds names then refuses each program that names a variable or a parameter after it.
- A `fail` without a static argument has the result type `Any`. Where it must have a type, write the static argument, as `strToInt` calls `fail[\ZZ32\]`.
- A dotted method shadows a top-level function of the same name (`overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading").
- In an api, declare each top-level function and each member of a trait or object at the header that the component gives it. A function's header is its name, its static parameters with their bounds, its modifiers, its `throws` clause, its parameters' modifiers and types, and its return type. A function's parameters' names and a `where` clause do not count, but each static parameter's name counts (ledger row 836). Give an object's value parameters the api's names, because they are its fields (`compiler.md`, "Traps of the compiled path"). In the cases below, change the component's header to the api's, not the api's to the component's. The examples are in `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` and `.fss`.
  - The member's body already answers the api's type. `RR64`'s `opr |\self/|`, `opr |/self\|` and `truncate` answer `ZZ64`, because their natives answer `ZZ64` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:540-547`).
  - The api cannot name the component's type. `Array2`'s and `Array3`'s `bounds` and `zeroIndices` answered types of `RangeInternals`, which depends on this api. They now answer the api's `CompactFullRange` types, which those types extend.
  - The api's type is wider, and the overrides and bodies use only that type. `DelegatedIndexed`'s `generator` answers the api's `Generator[\E\]`, as `FlatString`'s override does.

  In the api, write `abstract` on each member that the component leaves without a body.
- The compiled checker's export check matches each api member with a component member of the same name and header. It matches these members in these ways:
  - A field, as `x: ZZ32` in an api's trait: by a component field of its name, its type and its modifiers other than `var`. A component's getter does not match it, so declare a field in the component too (ledger row 842).
  - An object's value parameter: by its type and its modifiers other than `var`, but not by its name.
  - A getter written `abstract`, as `abstract getter one(): T`: by a component getter at its header, or by a component field of its name and type that is neither `hidden` nor `private`. A `hidden` field has no getter.
  - Another member written `abstract`: by a component member at the api's header, with a body or without one.

  Each entry of the check's error names a trait or object and only its first member that differs. After you fix that member, check again to see the next. These steps run the check:
  - For a component of a compiled program or test: `fortress compile`.
  - For the one library's `FortressLibrary` component: the count stage (`compiler.md`, "The checker's time").
  - For the other thirteen components that the gate's distance stage checks: that stage. When a rung needs it, the brief gives its command.
  - For another component of the one library: no step, until the switch-over.
- A new overload can make walk refuse every program at load (`interpreter.md`, "What walk checks").
- Write a new native as a public static method of a class under `nativeHelpers/`, and bind it with `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.Class.method")`. Both paths run it. Give it the Java types that carry the declared types (`interpreter.md`, "Natives"). Write a glue class under `interpreter/glue/prim/`, which only walk runs, only where no Java type carries a declared type, as for the bindings in `Library/Reflect.fss`. A native is an edit of Java: rebuild (`build-and-caches.md`, "Two layers of code"), and test it on both paths (`compiler.md`, "Natives").
- Check microGPT under walk as `interpreter.md`, "The model program", says.

## Editing

A comment after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span. It also becomes part of the unambiguous name made from the span. So a comment-only edit changes the syntax tree. Before you compare parse trees or diagnostics across such an edit, map their positions back to the lines before the edit. Three removed scripts did this: `parse-compare.sh`, `ast-compare.py` and `remap-lines.py`. Print one with `git show ab067d9b6^:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/<name>`.

# The specification

Three folders hold the team's specification:

- `Specification/` is the team's text, as the revival revises it. It says what the language means, except where a decision of the curator says otherwise.
- `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the unrevised copy. Cite it as "the Working Draft of February 2011". Only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Leave this copy unchanged.
- `Documentation/Specification/` is the team's later restart, which they did not finish. If its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, cite it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word.

Appendix I, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, records the changes to the text. Its revival section has one entry for each change that the revival made.

A draft build prints the team's `\note{}` boxes, and a release build hides them. Many say that a feature was not built, for example "Reduction variables are not yet supported." Before you record a missing feature as a gap, grep the notes of its chapter: `grep -n '\\note{' Specification/<file>.tex`.

The api listings of the library part are generated from the library's `.fsi` files when the specification is built (`Specification/library/apis/`, not in the tree). A listing shows the library itself, so it cannot justify a change of the library. Cite the `.fsi` file.

To weigh the specification against the team's later texts, or to find the designers' reason for a rule, read `exploring.md`, "Weighing the sources".

## Changing the text: the revision form

Every change of the text has the four parts below, so that no disagreement between the text and an implementation stays hidden.

1. An entry in the revival section of Appendix I: a `\subsection` with a `\seclabel`. The entry gives:
   - the affected sections, the change, its rationale and its effect. The effect names each departure: each way in which walk or the compiled path does not do what the new text says, with its ledger row.
   - the original text, quoted with its path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`;
   - what a reversal to the alternative not taken would need;
   - the decision of the curator that it follows (its POSITIONS entry), or the reason that your brief gives.

   For the form, print one entry, about 2 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:Specification/appendices/changes.tex#choice of a coercion'`.

2. At each changed passage, a callout that prints in every build, unlike a `\note`:

       \revision{<label>}{<what changed, in a sentence or two>}

   `<label>` is the `\seclabel` of the entry. `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex` defines `\revision`.

3. The front matter's one paragraph on the revision, in `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex`. If your change makes it false, correct it.

4. The full reasoning, in `decision-record.md` in the folder of your work under `explorations/`: each changed passage, the original and the new text, the reason, and the way back. For the form, print one passage of an earlier record, about 4 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md#3.3'`.

If the revision refuses an example, keep the example in the text, marked "Not allowed", as the specification itself does. If your change contradicts a calculus of Appendix A, keep the calculus's rules and soundness claims. Add a callout to it that says what it predates.

Check each changed sentence of `Specification/` or `Documentation/` against the curator's decisions. If it says what walk or the compiled path does, run a program that shows it.

## Building it

To check your LaTeX, build the specification in a built tree, after the setup lines. It takes about 90 s, so start it detached (`session.md`, "Long commands"):

    nohup bash -c '( cd Specification/fortress && ./ant genSource && ./ant tex ) > tmp/spec.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/spec.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &

- Both commands must end in `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, and `grep -c 'LaTeX Warning: Reference\|LaTeX Warning: Label .* multiply defined\|LaTeX Warning: There were multiply-defined labels\|^! Undefined control sequence' Specification/fortress/fortress.log` must print 0.
- If `pdflatex` is missing, install the packages of the `PKGS` line of `explorations/experiment/setup.sh` with `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y`.
- The build writes only ignored files, its log among them, which can reach 400 MB. Remove them afterwards: `git clean -fXq -- Specification`.
- Update `Specification/fortress.pdf` only if your brief asks for it: copy `Specification/fortress/fortress.pdf` over it.

## When the text and an implementation disagree

- If a decision of the curator says which side is correct, the other side is wrong. If the wrong side is in your area, change it to agree. If not, record the departure as `tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", says.
- If no decision says so, the disagreement is a conflict. Switch to exploring (`exploring.md`).
- If the passage has an Appendix I entry, name the departure or the conflict in the entry's effect, with its ledger row. Then the text claims no more than holds.

## Citing it

- If your change renames or removes a section that a test names, update that citation in the same commit.
- Inside the text, cite a section with `\secref{label}`.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The standard and the sources

POSITIONS.md:30
- P-33 **The work toward microGPT compiled follows the phases, in the order that the curator approved, and the rest of the switch-over takes microGPT's slice first.** These phases are steps of the work, not the compiler's phases, and they are numbered 3 to 6, after two earlier ones. Phase 3 ends when the compiled checker reports no error on the apis and components of the interpreter's library that the distance to the switch-over counts (F-53 defines the distance, says what it counts and holds its value). The library's other components are not part of phase 3: each is cleared before the first program that needs it, and at the latest before walk runs the checker (P-12), so `System` by the switch-over, since the compiler's tests need it (F-293); F-290 counts their errors. Phase 4, the switch-over: first the natives, the library's `builtinPrimitive` bindings made to run on the compiled path, then the compiled path reads the interpreter's library and the compiler's prelude is deleted; phase 5, microGPT compiles: its static types, the array design and the code generator's open gaps; phase 6, microGPT runs fast. The rest of phase 4 takes microGPT's slice first: the compile command selects the one library beside the prelude, one build serving both (F-381), so that each wall that only a tree switched onto the one library shows is met as one rung with its own test on `main`, under the gate, beside the code generator's walls; the move of the compiled tests and the prelude's deletion come last. Why: those walls stand one behind another (F-352), and this way gates each one, where the whole switch-over first lands them in one piece that no gate checks in parts. Code-generator work goes on beside that order, under either library (P-37). Row 320, an api implemented by a component of another name does not link, is part of the switch-over's design.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:35
- P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. Why: the switch-over spares porting the interpreter's library into the compiler's; the revival develops the checker until it accepts that fuller library. The curator sees the compiler's prelude, its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, as a bootstrap to remove. So no declaration is added to the compiler's prelude, and at the switch-over its three files are deleted and their tests kept (P-38 says which tests are respelled; F-293 holds the compiler's fourth file, `CompilerSystem`). There are two exceptions, each so that both paths do the same before the switch-over, and each copy goes with the prelude: the numerals, where the prelude carries the design of P-174 and P-176; and the built-in number types, where it takes the form of P-178. The decision settles which files survive, not the designs inside them: the one library takes a design of the prelude's where it is the team's later decision, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types. This decision does not stop work on the code generator, which is compiler work under either library.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Numbers

POSITIONS.md:107
- P-178 **Each built-in number type is one `value object` under its own name, and walk's native number objects `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `BigNum` and `UnsignedLong` go.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN64` and `RR64` are each declared `value object`, as `NN32` and `RR32` already are, in place of a trait with one native object below it, such as `trait ZZ32 comprises { Int }` with `value object Int extends ZZ32`. An object is a leaf, so no type of a program extends a built-in number type; a program's own number type extends `Number` (P-160). Compiled code can then hold a value of such a type as a bare JVM `int`, `long` or `double` (P-17), and both paths take this form before the switch-over: the one library by the merge, and the compiler's prelude by an exception to P-37, as for the numerals, which goes with the prelude. For the number types it replaces the pattern that P-164's reason names, a trait with walk's native object below it. Why: the two names are a duality between the two libraries, which the curator called a problem that the revival makes for itself by keeping it; the second names are walk's internals, which a program is not to see (P-167); and the compiler prelude's open trait let a program's object extend `ZZ32`, which a bare `int` cannot hold (row 866, such a program compiled and died when it ran). Detail: `reviews/carriers-ways-2026-11-13.md`, "Way D. One object per type: each number trait merged with its one object"; the merge as probed: `compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/number-object-merge.md`, "What was built".

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:74
- P-164 **The five I/O objects become plain Fortress objects, each over a Java-backed value in a field, of two traits that `FortressLibrary` declares, `JavaBufferedWriter` and `JavaBufferedReader`.** The two traits take the compiler prelude's names and methods; each method is a public native binding in P-58's form on a helper of `nativeHelpers/fileOps`, 17 bindings, 14 on existing helpers and 3 on new ones for standard output, standard error and standard input, with factories over a file name and for each standard stream. Walk's loader carries the two traits by name as the Java classes `FortressBufferedWriter` and `FortressBufferedReader`, through a private native object below each trait, and the checker's walk-world foreign-type table (`compiler/NamingCzar.java`) holds the two entries (F-330), since the checker reads the whole helper class that a binding names (F-321). `Writer`, `BufferedWriter`, `FileWriteStream`, `FileReadStream` and `Reader` leave their native components and each holds its Java-backed value in a field, as the team's `BirdyLib` `FileReadStream` does; `stdOut` stays a `Writer`, in UTF-8. Their 36 glue bindings are gone (F-330, F-332). At the switch-over, the run-time classes `FJavaBufferedWriter` and `FJavaBufferedReader` implement the one library's traits, and the boxed-type table's two entries and `fileOps`' raise strings name the one library's types. No model line changes. Why: it is the team's later shape for a file stream, an object over a Java-backed value in a field, with the team's Java types; it follows the library's pattern for a type that both paths name and that holds a Java value, a trait of the main component with walk's native object below it and the compiled path's run-time class implementing it, the pattern that the number types leave by P-178; and it maps one Java type to one Fortress type to one run-time class, as the checker's table requires, where the other ways leave the compiled half undesigned, decide nothing, or cost a third rung and split the standard output. P-162's pair pattern stays for the natives that no bare helper reaches. Detail: `reviews/io-objects-carrier-2026-11-06.md`, sections 1, 6 (b), 7 and 8.

POSITIONS.md:76
- P-169 **The runtime's own 13 native bindings, the arrays' store, threads with `abort` and the task trace, name compiled helpers that walk's loader answers with walk's own operations, P-167's device, in two compiled shapes.** Each keeps P-58's form, a bare `builtinPrimitive("…")` naming a helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the compiled path runs; walk's loader answers the name with walk's glue, so walk keeps its `AtomicArray` store and its `spawn`, and for these names P-58's walk half bends, as for P-167's two. The arrays' 7, of `PrimitiveArray`, `PrimImmutableArray` and `PrimImmutableRR64Array`: the compiled half by P-164's device, a store trait in `FortressLibrary` whose bindings name helpers of a new `nativeHelpers/arrayOps` over a compiled class that holds the elements; `PrimitiveArray` and `PrimImmutableArray` leave the native component and hold the store in a field, and walk's native object below the trait holds an `AtomicArray`; `PrimImmutableRR64Array`'s two are on a compiled `double[]` class that no factory chooses until array decision A (P-84, P-85; F-333). The compiled store is an `Object[]`, and the compiled transaction tracks its reads and writes by the array and the index (`TXReadSlot`, `TXWriteSlot`): P-84 stores every number type's array unboxed, so a compiled `atomic` write into any array needs that keying, and an array of objects keeps one box an element, not two. Threads, `abort` and the task trace, 6: helpers in a `nativeHelpers` class over the compiled runtime, as the team's `nativeHelpers/runtime.java` is (F-335); `Thread`'s `val`, `wait`, `ready` and `stop` raise until the code generator compiles `spawn` (row 82). The numerals' 24 bindings, `IntLiteral`'s 21 and `FloatLiteral`'s 3, left the library with those two types (P-174), so no carrier is designed for them; `IntLiteral`'s other 8, its conversions and comparisons, left with it. A test on both paths holds the two halves together where both run. Why: every array, vector, varargs list and `args` of the one library is built on `PrimitiveArray` or `PrimImmutableArray`, and a body left on glue compiles to the library's own `builtinPrimitive`, which fails, so by the code's reading a compiled program would raise at its first array; walk's loader carries no element, `Thread` or literal (F-299), and an `Object` carrier would take walk's array writes out of walk's transactions. == explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, ## Landed semantics

FACTS.md:290
- F-388 **The compiler's prelude declares its seven number types as value objects, whose classes the code generator writes over the run time's payload classes.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `RR32` and `RR64` are `value object`s in `CompilerBuiltin`; each object's class extends the abstract payload class `compiler/runtimeValues/F<T>`, which holds the JVM value. Descriptors, stamped instances and the RTTI's `className()` name the type by the payload class, while the RTTI's class stays the object's, so that the type lies below its traits at run time; a dotted call casts its receiver to the object's class; `F<T>.make` reaches the object's class's `make` by the name that `LibraryNames` gives, for the prelude only (the one library's seven have no rows yet, fork N4). So a program's object below a number type is refused at the compile, an overloading at `ZZ32` beside one at a program's trait is valid, a `typecase` clause at such a trait over a number is refused as unreachable (row 1081), and a number type named as a value does not compile (row 1082). Tests: `compiler_tests/NumberObjectsCompiled.test`, `compiler_tests/XXXNumberTypeExtendRefusedCompiled.test`, `compiler_tests/ComprisesMeetGenericTrait.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-number-payload-objects/REPORT.md`, "The design as built (a point to report)".

== explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, ## The checker and the one library

FACTS.md:177
- F-381 **The compile command reads the one library where `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one` (or `-Dfortress.library=one`) selects it, keeps its caches in `default_repository/caches-one`, and its tests run in `testFast`'s onelibrary track.** The selection is read once per JVM (`ProjectProperties.compiledPathUsesOneLibrary`); `Shell.useCompilerLibraries()` follows it, and the two class path scripts follow the variable only. Unset, every command reads the prelude as before. A program compiled under the selection does not run yet, since the one library has no jars (F-34; row 1062). Tests: `ProjectFortress/one_library_tests/OneLibraryHalf.test`, `OneLibraryPrintBig.test` and `XXXOneLibraryRunHalf.test`, run by `ant testOneLibrary` and by `ant testFast`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-library-selector/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why", "The tests: the failing run on the base, the passing run" and "Wrong pairings, and the run under the selection".

FACTS.md:172
- F-353 **One build can serve the compiled path with either library, shown in a scratch tree: the prelude's thirteen run-time value classes stay, and a second set under the same names, in a second class folder that the class path puts first, serves the one library.** The scratch tree is that of F-352 with its hacks, nine of them behind a selector that one environment variable sets at the compile and at the run. One JVM serves one library. There the one-line program runs against both libraries, and the `Array1` program and the dot loop against the one library, by hand and through `fortress junit`. ### Way C. The object's class carries the value, and the trait stays an interface

This is walk's way, brought to the compiled path. The library's text does not change.

**On `ZZ32`.** The declarations stay as they are today. The code generator compiles them as it compiles any trait and object, with one addition for a native object:

    interface fortress/FortressLibrary$ZZ32                      (from trait ZZ32)
    final class fortress/FortressBuiltin$Int implements ...$ZZ32 (from value object Int)
        final int val;
        static Int make(int)        int getValue()

- The carrier is `Int`'s class. It has `asFloat`'s body, because `Int` declares it. So W13 does not arise.
- `Int extends ZZ32` names the interface, as every `extends` clause does. Nothing extends a carrier, because nothing extends an object. So W14 does not arise.
- A table gives each native object its payload: `Int` an `int`, `Float` a `double`, `FlatString` a `java.lang.String`, `BigNum` a `BigInteger`. This is the table of `NamingCzar` today, keyed by the object.
- One rule answers W12: a value of a native object is read at its trait where a static argument is formed, and the stamped class is named by the carrier. Walk has this rule (F-344). The checker already lets a value of `trait T comprises { O }` stand where `O` is expected (the rehearsal's W7).
- A value of static type `ZZ32` is exactly an `Int`, because the trait says `comprises { Int }`. So a descriptor for `ZZ32` may name `Int`'s class, as a descriptor names `FZZ32` today. The cast that row 307 asks for is the same knowledge.

**On `Boolean`.** `value object Boolean` compiles to its own class, with a `boolean` payload. Its methods written in Fortress (`cond`, `generate`, `=`) are the object's methods. No trait, no second name.

**On `String`.** `String` is an interface. `FlatString`'s class holds a `java.lang.String`. `CatString`, `EmptyString` and `SubString` are plain classes. A helper's Java `String` result becomes a `FlatString` value. The wrapper generator reads a helper's Java `String` parameter as the trait `String` (`NamingCzar.java:484`), so the wrapper casts it to `FlatString`'s class: the rehearsal's new converter. The cast is safe because the library's bindings pass a `FlatString` there: walk refuses a helper parameter declared `String` other than `self` (the skill's `references/interpreter.md`, "Natives"). The table could read such a parameter as `FlatString` instead. This is the same in every way.

**On `Float`.** `Float`'s class holds a `double` and has its 146 lines as its own methods. `RR64` is an interface. A call `x + y` on two `RR64` values dispatches to `Float`'s `+`, as under walk.

**Where the class comes from: three forms.** This choice is inside way C.

1. Written by hand, extending the object's generated springboard, as `FZZ32` extends the trait's today. It needs the stub files, and `FlatString` cannot be stubbed in Java (the rehearsal's W2: Java allows no class `FlatString` nested in a class `FlatString`).
2. Written by the code generator, over a small payload class written by hand: `abstract class FZZ32 extends FValue { final int val; getValue() }`, and the generated `Int extends FZZ32`. No stub is needed, because the hand-written class extends nothing generated. The run time's Java keeps a name to test, as `nativeHelpers/equalityRule.java:38` tests `instanceof FZZ32`. The object then takes its traits' default methods by forwarding methods, which the code generator already writes for every trait after the first (`CodeGen.java:888-909`).
3. Written whole by the code generator, with the payload as a hidden field. The run time's Java then reaches the payload through a small interface.

Form 2 looks best to me: no stubs, and the box's chain of constructors is three classes, `Int`, `FZZ32`, `FValue`. Today's chain through the one library's springboards is six, which leaves a margin of two frames before HotSpot stops removing temporary boxes (F-302). Not measured.

**What blocks it.** The code generator compiles an object without value parameters as a singleton, one instance. A native object has many values. The specification leaves a native component's meaning to the implementation, and walk uses that freedom in the same place. So the block is in the code generator only, and it gets around it as walk does: by the component's `native` mark and a table.

**What it changes.**

- The library's text: nothing. (`NN32`'s `zero` and `one`, the rehearsal's W4, are a defect apart.)
- Walk: nothing.
- The code generator: a native object gets a payload, `make` and `getValue`, and many instances; the tables are keyed by the object; a trait with one comprised native object is named by that object's class in descriptors; the wrapper generator's converters read the same table. About three rungs, the rehearsal's own estimate for W2's repair, with W12's rule among them.
- The run-time classes: the thirteen become payload classes (form 2) or are re-parented (form 1). `equalityRule`, `FValue.asString`, `Utility` and `FException` name the new classes. The helpers' 99 raise strings change in every way.
- The loader: the run's copy of the table (`Naming.java`), and one canonical name for a stamp.
- The tests: the compiled tests stay. New tests: `typecase x of Int`, `Box(3)` as a `Box[\ZZ32\]` compiled, a program's `object MyNum extends ZZ32` refused by the checker (row 866's test promoted).

**Speed later.** It helps.

- The type is closed in the language itself. So "a value of static type `RR64` is a `double`" is sound, and the code generator can choose unboxed arithmetic by static type (PLAN's phase 6, decision B; P-17).
- In a field: a field declared `RR64` in a plain object can become a `double` field. A field of type `T` in `Box[\T\]` needs the loader to stamp a different class (F-18); the canonical name of W12's rule is what it would key on.
- In an array: the store is already a `double[]` (`JavaRR64ArrayStore`, F-333; P-84). The carrier decides only which box `get` returns until phase 6.
- Across a call: a function `f(x: RR64): RR64` can take the descriptor `(D)D`, because no other class can arrive.
- Dispatch on a built-in type tests one final class, as today. With the closed type, the test can be dropped where the static type is the trait.
- The team's bytecode optimizer finds a box by the methods `make` and `getValue` on a carried type (`compiler/asmbytecodeoptimizer/MethodInsn.java:71-85`). Way C keeps both names.

**Undo.** Cheap. The library and walk are untouched. Going to way D later is additive. Going to way A later costs what way A costs today.

**The team's texts.** For: the interpreter's library as written; walk's native components; the specification's value objects and its `trait Boolean ... comprises { ... }`; Chase's unboxing plan of 2009, whose cases are objects and `comprises`. Against: the prelude and its run time put the class on the trait.

## 2. How the library is selected

One variable, `FORTRESS_LIBRARY`. Unset, everything is as today. With `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`:

- **At the compile.** `WellKnownNames.compiledPathUsesOneLibrary` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/WellKnownNames.java`) reads the variable once for the JVM (or `-Dfortress.library=one`). `Shell.useCompilerLibraries()` (`Shell.java`), which every compiled-path command calls, points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` at the one library's names where it is set, and at the prelude's where not.
- **At the run.** `bin/fortress_classpath` puts `ProjectFortress/build-one`, the second set's classes, before `ProjectFortress/build`. `bin/run_classpath` builds on that script, so the run's JVM finds the second set's `FZZ32` first. The compile's JVM gets the same class path.
- **The caches.** A caches folder holds one library's jars and the programs compiled against it, so the one library has its own: `default_repository/caches-one`, named by hand in `FORTRESS_CACHES`.

One JVM serves one library: `NamingCzar`'s tables are filled once, when the class loads, as on the base (`NamingCzar.fortLib`). The harness fits this: its `run` step is a process of its own that inherits the environment, so a test track against the one library is the same harness started with the three settings.

| the stores' carriers `FJavaArrayStore`, `FJavaRR64ArrayStore`; the stubs `fortress/FortressLibrary.java`, `FortressBuiltin.java`, `FlatStringC.java` | `ProjectFortress/src-one/` | in the second set only |
| the helpers' 99 raise strings, and the six of `FortressBufferedReader` and `FortressBufferedWriter` | `runtimeValues/LibraryNames.java`, one copy in each set; `Utility.java` calls it | the strings stay the prelude's; the second set's copy maps them |
| the compile's table of carried types (the rehearsal's 15 rows) | `compiler/NamingCzar.java` | entered only where the one library is selected, since each row also enters the type's bare name (`NamingCzar.b`), and a test's own `Float` or `Char` would be taken for a carried type |
| a carried parent named by its interface (W14); `FlatString`'s class named `fortress/FlatStringC` | `compiler/NamingCzar.java` | by the variable |

== explorations/compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/probe-y.md:80-91

## 3. The hacks

Each is marked `PROBE Y` in the patch. The rehearsal's twelve are all still in the tree and are not repeated here; nine of them are now behind the variable.

1. **The selector is an environment variable read in two places** (`WellKnownNames`, `bin/fortress_classpath`). Proper form: one selector, say an option of the commands that the scripts pass on, or a mark in the program's jar that the run reads, so that a program compiled against one library cannot be run on the other's classes. Today a wrong pairing fails at load with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
2. **The one library's caches folder is named by hand.** Proper form: `ProjectProperties.CACHES` and the two scripts take the folder from the selection; `ant cleanCache` and the build's stamp know both folders. Today the build stamps and empties only `default_repository/caches`, so the one library's jars go stale without notice after an edit of the code generator.
3. **The second set's sources are made by string replacement in `build.xml`,** one rule a whole clause of one file. Proper form: it depends on the carriers' decision. If the two sets stay equal up to names, the map can stand as a small table; if the one library's carriers get content of their own, they are hand-written files in `src-one`.
4. **The raise strings are mapped by prefix** (`LibraryNames.exceptionClass`): `fortress.CompilerBuiltin$X` and `fortress.CompilerLibrary$X` to `fortress.FortressLibrary$X`. Proper form: a helper names an exception by its simple name, and each set's `LibraryNames` gives the component. That edits the 105 strings once, with no change of behaviour for the prelude.
5. **The guards around the rehearsal's hacks** (`if (!compiledPathUsesOneLibrary) throw __t`, and the like). They go when the hacks they guard are repaired.
6. **`Naming.java`'s table and the converters hold both libraries' rows.** Harmless by their keys. Proper form: they follow the selection as `NamingCzar`'s does, from one table.
7. **The build's stamp does not cover `build-one`** (`build.xml`, `implementationFingerprint`). Proper form: it does.
8. **The verifier is off for every run against the one library,** as in the rehearsal (W7). With it on, `Hello` dies as there: 'VerifyError: Bad type on operand stack … FortressLibrary$QQ$DefaultTraitMethods'.

### W2. The wrappers of the helper classes (row 874)

`fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss`:

    java.lang.RuntimeException: Can't generate header for method floatToString with jvm desc =Ljava/lang/String; stripped = FortressLibrary$String

Row 874 holds it, as PLAN's N5 says. It is not one table but the question of which run-time class carries each of the one library's built-in types on the compiled path. The record does not hold that design; PLAN names only `FlatString`'s carrier as unmeasured. What the hack had to decide (all of it `SWITCH HACK`):

- `NamingCzar`'s table of types that a hand-written class carries, and `Naming`'s copy of it for the run: `FortressLibrary`'s `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `RR64`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `JavaBufferedReader`, `JavaBufferedWriter` to `FZZ32`, `FZZ64`, `FRR64`, `FNN64`, `FZZ`, `FJavaBufferedReader`, `FJavaBufferedWriter`; `FortressBuiltin`'s `Boolean`, `RR32`, `NN32`, `Char` to `FBoolean`, `FRR32`, `FNN32`, `FCharacter`; `FlatString`'s `FlatString` to `FJavaString`.
- The wrapper generator's converters (`FortressMethodAdapter`): a helper's Java `String` is read as the trait `String`, which no class carries (a `CatString` is a `String` too), so the wrapper takes the trait's interface and casts to `FJavaString`; a new converter. A helper's Java `Object` at `Any` had no converter either ('stripped = AnyType$Any', met at `arrayOps.get`); a second new converter.
- The array stores (met as its own failure, 'Can't generate header for method make with jvm desc =Lcom/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FortressArrayStore; stripped = FortressLibrary$JavaArrayStore'): `FortressArrayStore` and `FortressRR64ArrayStore` are plain Java classes outside the Fortress hierarchy, so `JavaArrayStore` and `JavaRR64ArrayStore` have no compiled value. Two new run-time classes, `FJavaArrayStore` and `FJavaRR64ArrayStore`, each a store in a field. F-333 says the stores are built; they are, but nothing carries one as a Fortress value on the compiled path.
- The run-time classes extend the prelude's generated classes by name in their Java source (`FZZ32 extends fortress.CompilerBuiltin.ZZ32.DefaultTraitMethods`), against bootstrap stubs in `ProjectFortress/src/fortress/CompilerBuiltin.java`. Thirteen classes re-parented onto the one library's traits, with new stubs `fortress/FortressLibrary.java`, `FortressBuiltin.java` and `FlatStringC.java`; `FValue.asString` and `Utility.makeFortressException` name the one library's `String`; the helpers' 99 raise strings name `fortress.FortressLibrary$…` (30 `DivisionByZero`, 55 `IntegerOverflow`, 11 `IOFailure`, 2 `FileNotFoundException`, 1 `FailCalled`).
- Five of the carried types are objects in the one library, where the prelude has traits: `value object Boolean`, `RR32`, `NN32`, `Char` (`FortressBuiltin.fss`) and `object FlatString` (`FlatString.fss`). A hand-written class can extend a trait's generated `DefaultTraitMethods`, whose methods take `self` as a parameter and cast it; an object's class is final and its methods read `this`. The hack makes the five traits in the scratch library, each with `comprises { XCarrier }` and an empty object `XCarrier`, so that the checker keeps the exclusions that an object has (without the clause the apis fail the overloading check: 15 errors, such as 'Invalid overloading of || in trait FlatString: (FlatString, Char)->String and (String, Number)->String'). This breaks walk in the scratch tree, which binds these objects' natives.
- `FlatString`'s classes cannot be stubbed in Java under the component's name, since Java source allows no class `FlatString` nested in a class `FlatString`, and they are outside the package `fortress`, where a Java class of a named package cannot reach them. The hack names the component's class `fortress/FlatStringC`.

A real repair is a design first (the carriers: which class is a `ZZ32`, given `trait ZZ32 comprises { Int }` with `value object Int` in `FortressBuiltin`; what a `String` is at a helper; whether the five objects stay objects, with the code generator taught to let a hand-written class be an object's class), then about three rungs: the tables with the converters and the stores' carriers; the run-time classes with their stubs and the raise strings; the object carriers. PLAN sizes N5 as one rung inside the names batch.

== explorations/coordinator/map/compile-path-walkthrough.md:501-585

## 6. The run: the second JVM and the class loader

**The second JVM.** `bin/fortress run` hands off to `bin/run`, which launches
`com.sun.fortress.runtimeSystem.MainWrapper` (`bin/fortress:16-18`,
`bin/run:41`). The class path puts `bytecode_cache`, `bytecode_cache/*` and
`nativewrapper_cache` **ahead** of the tool class path
(`bin/run_classpath:26`).

**The trap in that ordering.** If the library jars are not in
`bytecode_cache`, the loader silently falls back to frozen stubs compiled from
checked-in Java sources into `ProjectFortress/build/fortress/` — an older
snapshot of `CompilerBuiltin` — and the program dies with a
`NoSuchMethodError` on a method that plainly exists in the `.fss`
(`repo-internals.md:162-182`; `modules-and-phases.md` B.13). The cure is to
compile the five library components in order first; the recipe is in
`repo-internals.md:170-180`. This is a cache problem misread as a compiler bug
for years (`repo-internals.md:152-160`).

**What `MainWrapper` does.** It first stashes the program's arguments in a
static field rather than passing them. It then initializes the named component's
class, and the class of each component that it uses, through
`InstantiatingClassloader.ONLY`, in a root task (F-348). Then it invokes the
named class's no-argument `main` (`runtimeSystem/MainWrapper.java:19, 30-46,
94-98`, at climb batch 30's landing, `d89fc0fda4`).

**The class loader is where compiled Fortress stops being ordinary bytecode.**
`InstantiatingClassloader.loadClass` (2,946 lines in the file; the method at
`runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:178`) examines the class *name*
for markers and, for most of them, **generates** the class instead of reading
it (`:227-296`):

- a tuple RTTI class, an arrow RTTI class (`:227-232`);
- a generic function instance, by reading the template and rewriting it
  (`:233-242`);
- a closure (`:243-244`);
- for a name in oxford or angle brackets: arrow interfaces and their abstract
  and wrapped forms, tuple types, concrete and "any" tuples, union types, and —
  the general case — an instantiation of a generic template
  (`:245-280`);
- an RTTI class, translated to flush out symbolic references (`:281-290`);
- otherwise, the bytes as they are (`:292-294`).

**What the rewriting is.** `Instantiater` is an ASM `ClassVisitor` holding two
substitution maps, one for types and one for operators; `visit` replaces the
class's own name, its superclass and each interface with the substituted name
(`runtimeSystem/Instantiater.java:26-38, 47-58`). The bracket and mangling
conventions are `runtimeSystem/Naming.java` (1,203 lines).

**What it does not do.** *Instantiation renames; it does not change
representation* (`modules-and-phases.md` B.11, and the same conclusion in the
map's summary, `map/README.md` §2). There is no mechanism for giving one
instantiation a different field shape from another: the expando hook that would
do it is a stub, `if (false) { // Here will go all the magic expando-stuff. }`
(`InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-171`). A probe in the array review confirms
that stamping cannot produce a `double[]` field
(`array-design-review.md` Q4).

**What it does with a size in a type, today.** The compiler mangles a size into
the instantiation name: `NamingCzar` maps `KindNat` and each `IntArg` to the
tag `Naming.XL_INTNAT` (`compiler/NamingCzar.java:1826-1832`, `:1888-1910`).
Nothing reads it back. The runtime's generic RTTI class holds one field per
static parameter, all typed as type RTTI, and the only kind the runtime
consults is `opr` (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:1600-1622`;
`Naming.java:95-108`); `XL_INTNAT` is declared at `Naming.java:213` and that is
its only runtime mention. Measured consequence: a `nat` used in *value*
position compiles to a `getstatic` of a class the loader cannot produce and
dies at run time with `NoClassDefFoundError`
(`array-design-review.md` §1b, probe 6). And the code generator refuses a size
in an `extends` clause before that, with
`CompilerError("Only emitting RTTI for types right now")`
(`CodeGen.java:5793`).

**The rest of the runtime.** A compiled program's entry class extends
`FortressExecutable`, whose static initializer creates one work-stealing pool
sized by `FORTRESS_THREADS` (`runtimeSystem/FortressExecutable.java:22-56`).
Transactions are static methods on `BaseTask` that generated code calls
(`runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java:180-260`). Both are duplicated: the interpreter
has its own independent task and transaction implementations under
`interpreter/evaluator/` (`modules-and-phases.md` B.11), so a fix in one is not
a fix in the other. Two one-line defects on this side — an eagerly built debug
string in `BaseTask.inATransaction()` and a float literal kept as a `String`
and re-parsed per use — were repaired on 2026-09-17 and are on record with
their before/after numbers (FACTS, execution model).

### Forks the batch takes

Each fork below builds within a decision on record or chooses where the record leaves an implementation open, and each can be undone. For a fork that leaves a form unbuilt, it says what a program that writes the form gets.

#!/bin/bash
# lib14.sh <tree>: the one library's fourteen components compiled to jars under FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one, one by one,
# in the rehearsal's order (plan-31/probes/switch-rehearsal.md, section 4), into <tree>/default_repository/caches-one;
# each line: the component, its exit status, its seconds; then the jars. A component's jar is deleted first, since a
# compile of an unchanged source whose jar exists writes nothing. Run from anywhere, after the setup lines.
T=$(cd "$1" && pwd); cd "$T/ProjectFortress" || exit 2
export FORTRESS_HOME=$T FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one
for c in LibraryBuiltin/AnyType LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin ../Library/FortressLibrary ../Library/RangeInternals \
         LibraryBuiltin/NativeArray ../Library/FlatString ../Library/String ../Library/List ../Library/Stream \
         LibraryBuiltin/NatReflect ../Library/TypeProxy ../Library/Writer ../Library/CovariantCollection ../Library/OneShotFlag; do
  n=$(basename $c)
  rm -f "$T/default_repository/caches-one/bytecode_cache/$n.jar" "$T/default_repository/caches-one/bytecode_cache/fortress.$n.jar"
  s=$(date +%s)
  ../bin/fortress compile $c.fss > "$T/tmp/lib14-$n.txt" 2>&1
  rc=$?
  echo "$n rc=$rc seconds=$(( $(date +%s) - s ))"
done
ls -la "$T"/default_repository/caches-one/bytecode_cache/ | grep '\.jar' | awk '{print $5, $9}'
#!/bin/bash
# runprog.sh <tree> <Program>...: each program of plan-34/probes/programs compiled under FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one in
# <tree>/tmp/progs, then run twice, with the JVM's verifier on and with it off (the rehearsal's flags); prints each
# step's exit status and the run's last lines. Run after the setup lines.
T=$(cd "$1" && pwd); shift
HERE=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)
export FORTRESS_HOME=$T FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one
mkdir -p "$T/tmp/progs"; cd "$T/tmp/progs"
for p in "$@"; do
  cp "$HERE/programs/$p.fss" .
  rm -f "$T"/default_repository/caches-one/bytecode_cache/$p.jar
  "$T/bin/fortress" compile $p.fss > $p.compile.txt 2>&1; echo "$p compile rc=$?"; tail -3 $p.compile.txt | cut -c1-400
  "$T/bin/fortress" run $p > $p.on.txt 2>&1; echo "$p run, verifier on, rc=$?"; head -12 $p.on.txt | cut -c1-400
  JAVA_FLAGS="$JAVA_FLAGS -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:-BytecodeVerificationRemote" "$T/bin/fortress" run $p > $p.off.txt 2>&1
  echo "$p run, verifier off, rc=$?"; head -12 $p.off.txt | cut -c1-400
done

</delete>
  </target>

  <target name="cleanCache"
          description="Delete any cached Fortress ASTs in the development tree">
    <delete dir="${cache0}"/>
    <delete dir="${cache1}"/>
    <delete dir="${cacheOne}"/>
    <!-- Empty caches belong to the implementation now built: start them
         with its stamp, so that the next compileAll keeps what fills them. -->
    <loadfile property="cleanCache.stamp" srcFile="${build}/implementation.stamp"
              quiet="true">
      <filterchain><striplinebreaks/></filterchain>
    </loadfile>
    <stampCache dir="${cache0}" stamp="${cleanCache.stamp}" if:set="cleanCache.stamp"/>
    <stampCache dir="${cache1}" stamp="${cleanCache.stamp}" if:set="cleanCache.stamp"/>
    <stampCache dir="${cacheOne}" stamp="${cleanCache.stamp}" if:set="cleanCache.stamp"/>
  </target>

  <target name="cleanScala"
          description="Delete scalac-generated files in the development tree">
    <delete dir="${scalabuild}"/>
    <delete file="${build}/implementation.stamp"/>
  </target>

  <!--
       The caches and the implementation.

       The caches (${cache0}, ${cache1}, ${cacheOne}, and the private ones the tests use)
       hold what the implementation made from Fortress code: parsed and
       analysed ASTs, walk's rewritten ASTs and environments, compiled jars,
       native wrappers.  Fortress checks an entry against its Fortress sources,
       by date, and never against the implementation, so the build decides
       whether the caches still belong to the implementation:

       - ${build}/implementation.stamp is a SHA-1 over the implementation as it
         runs: every file of ${build}, ${PF}/third_party and bin, and
         default_repository/configuration, each with its relative path, and
         the JDK's version.  compileAll writes it last, after a successful
         build, and deletes it first.
       - A caches folder holds the stamp of the implementation it belongs to.
         At its end, compileAll keeps a caches folder only if that stamp equals
         the new build's: the implementation is byte for byte the one that
         filled it.  Otherwise it deletes the folder and starts it again, empty,
         with the new stamp.
       - ${build}/implementation.sources is a SHA-1 over what the build is made
         from: ${PF}/src (class files aside), ${PF}/astgen, ${PF}/third_party,
         bin, build.xml and default_repository/configuration, and the JDK's
         version.  When it differs at the start of compileAll, the build may
         change the implementation, so the caches are deleted before anything
         compiles, as cleanCache did here before: a build that then fails
         leaves no caches behind.  So are they when the build directory is no
         longer what the last build left (something else compiled into it).
       - scalac runs only when its inputs (the sources) or the build directory
         differ from what the last successful build left; for the same inputs
         its output is the same, byte for byte.

       ant cleanCache deletes the caches whatever their stamp; ant clean
       deletes the build too.
  -->

  <!-- One SHA-1 over the contents and relative paths of the nested files,
       with the JDK's version, into the property @{property}. -->
  <macrodef name="fingerprint">
    <attribute name="property"/>
    <element name="files" implicit="yes"/>
    <sequential>
      <delete dir="${build}/.fingerprint" quiet="true"/>
      <checksum algorithm="SHA-1" todir="${build}/.fingerprint"
                totalproperty="@{property}.sha1" forceoverwrite="yes">
        <files/>
      </checksum>
      <delete dir="${build}/.fingerprint" quiet="true"/>
      <property name="@{property}"
                value="${@{property}.sha1} java ${java.runtime.version}"/>
    </sequential>
  </macrodef>

  <!-- What the build is made from. -->
  <macrodef name="sourcesFingerprint">
    <attribute name="property"/>
    <sequential>
      <fingerprint property="@{property}">
        <fileset dir="${basedir}">
          <include name="${PF}/src/**"/>
          <include name="${PF}/astgen/**"/>
          <include name="${PF}/third_party/**"/>
          <include name="bin/**"/>
          <include name="build.xml"/>
          <include name="default_repository/configuration"/>
          <exclude name="${PF}/src/**/*.class"/>
        </fileset>
      </fingerprint>
    </sequential>
  </macrodef>

  <!-- The implementation as it runs. -->
  <macrodef name="implementationFingerprint">
    <attribute name="property"/>
    <sequential>
      <fingerprint property="@{property}">
        <fileset dir="${basedir}">
          <include name="${PF}/build/**"/>
          <include name="${PF}/third_party/**"/>
          <include name="bin/**"/>
          <include name="default_repository/configuration"/>
          <exclude name="${PF}/build/scalac-compileAll.args"/>
          <exclude name="${PF}/build/implementation.*"/>
          <exclude name="${PF}/build/.fingerprint/**"/>
        </fileset>
      </fingerprint>
    </sequential>
  </macrodef>

  <!-- Keep the caches folder @{dir} if it holds the stamp @{stamp};
       otherwise delete it, and, if it is a repository's caches folder,
       start it again, empty, with that stamp. -->
  <macrodef name="stampCache">
    <attribute name="dir"/>
    <attribute name="stamp"/>
    <sequential>
      <local name="cache.stamp"/>
      <local name="cache.kept"/>
      <local name="cache.parent"/>
      <local name="cache.restart"/>
      <loadfile property="cache.stamp" srcFile="@{dir}/implementation.stamp"
                quiet="true">
        <filterchain><striplinebreaks/></filterchain>
      </loadfile>
      <condition property="cache.kept">
        <equals arg1="${cache.stamp}" arg2="@{stamp}"/>
      </condition>
      <dirname property="cache.parent" file="@{dir}"/>
      <condition property="cache.restart">
        <and>
          <not><isset property="cache.kept"/></not>
          <available file="${cache.parent}/configuration"/>
        </and>
      </condition>
      <delete dir="@{dir}" unless:set="cache.kept"/>
      <mkdir dir="@{dir}" if:set="cache.restart"/>
      <echo file="@{dir}/implementation.stamp" message="@{stamp}${line.separator}"
            if:set="cache.restart"/>
      <echo message="Caches @{dir} kept" if:set="cache.kept"/>
      <echo message="Caches @{dir} started again, empty" if:set="cache.restart"/>
    </sequential>
  </macrodef>

  <!-- Read what the last successful build left, delete its stamps (they
       come back at the end of a successful compileAll), and delete the caches
       now if the sources or the build directory changed since that build, or
       the caches do not belong to it. -->
  <target name="checkCaches" depends="init">
    <sourcesFingerprint property="sources.start"/>
    <implementationFingerprint property="implementation.found"/>
    <loadfile property="built.sources" srcFile="${build}/implementation.sources"
              quiet="true">
      <filterchain><striplinebreaks/></filterchain>
    </loadfile>
    <loadfile property="built.stamp" srcFile="${build}/implementation.stamp"
              quiet="true">
      <filterchain><striplinebreaks/></filterchain>
    </loadfile>
    <loadfile property="cache0.stamp" srcFile="${cache0}/implementation.stamp"
              quiet="true">
      <filterchain><striplinebreaks/></filterchain>
    </loadfile>
    <loadfile property="cache1.stamp" srcFile="${cache1}/implementation.stamp"
              quiet="true">
      <filterchain><striplinebreaks/></filterchain>
    </loadfile>
    <loadfile property="cacheOne.stamp" srcFile="${cacheOne}/implementation.stamp"
              quiet="true">
      <filterchain><striplinebreaks/></filterchain>
    </loadfile>
    <condition property="sources.unchanged">
      <and>
        <equals arg1="${sources.start}" arg2="${built.sources}"/>
        <equals arg1="${implementation.found}" arg2="${built.stamp}"/>
      </and>
    </condition>
    <condition property="cache0.keep">
      <and>
        <isset property="sources.unchanged"/>
        <equals arg1="${cache0.stamp}" arg2="${built.stamp}"/>
      </and>
    </condition>
    <condition property="cache1.keep">
      <and>
        <isset property="sources.unchanged"/>
        <equals arg1="${cache1.stamp}" arg2="${built.stamp}"/>
      </and>
    </condition>
    <condition property="cacheOne.keep">
      <and>
        <isset property="sources.unchanged"/>
        <equals arg1="${cacheOne.stamp}" arg2="${built.stamp}"/>
      </and>
    </condition>
    <delete file="${build}/implementation.stamp"/>
    <delete file="${build}/implementation.sources"/>

  <!-- Generation of Operators.java depends only on the files listed below.
       Note that there are class files it depends on; if these class files are
       not up to date with respect to their sources, they are themselves
       recompiled by the compileCommon target.-->
  <target name="checkOperatorsUptodate" depends="init, compileCommon">
    <condition property="operators.uptodate">
      <and>
        <uptodate srcfile="${unicode.third}/UnicodeData.500.txt"
                  targetfile="${precedenceResolver}/Operators.java"/>
        <uptodate srcfile="${precedenceResolver}/operators.txt"
                  targetfile="${precedenceResolver}/Operators.java"/>
        <uptodate srcfile="${unicodeBuild}/OperatorStuffGenerator.class"
                  targetfile="${precedenceResolver}/Operators.java"/>
        <uptodate srcfile="${unicodeBuild}/Element.class"
                  targetfile="${precedenceResolver}/Operators.java"/>
      </and>
    </condition>
    <echo message="Operators up to date? ${operators.uptodate}"/>
  </target>

  <target name="operatorsGen"  unless="operators.uptodate"
          depends="init, compileCommon, checkOperatorsUptodate"
          description="Automatically generate visitors for AST nodes.">
    <echo message="Regenerating operators"/>
    <java classname="${package.prefix}.unicode.OperatorStuffGenerator"
          fork="true">
      <classpath>
        <pathelement location="${build}"/>
        <pathelement location="${PF}/third_party/plt/plt.jar"/>
      </classpath>
    </java>
  </target>

  <target name="DumpProperties"
          description="Dump properties as seen by a Java program.">
    <java classname="${package.prefix}.repository.DumpProperties"
          fork="true">
      <sysproperty key="DEBUG" value="true"/>
      <classpath>
        <pathelement location="${build}"/>
      </classpath>
    </java>
  </target>

  <target name="checkAstgen">
    <condition property="astgenerators.uptodate">
      <uptodate targetfile="${PF}/build/com/sun/fortress/astgen/FortressAstGenerator.class">
        <srcfiles dir="${PF}/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/" includes="*.java"/>
      </uptodate>
    </condition>
  </target>

  <target name="astGenerators"
          unless="astgenerators.uptodate"
          depends="init,checkAstgen"
          description="Compile all ASTGen custom generators.">
    <depend srcdir="${astgen.generators.src}"
            destdir="${build}"
            closure="yes"
            cache="${PF}/.dependencies"/>
    <javac encoding="UTF-8" 
        srcdir="${astgen.generators.src}"
        destdir="${build}"
        source="${javaSourceVersion}"
        target="${javaSourceVersion}"
        debug="true"
        includeantruntime="false"
        fork="true"
        memorymaximumsize="${junitMem}">
      <!-- Uncomment the following line to print unchecked warnings
           (here and in the 'compileCommon' target. -->
      <!-- <compilerarg value="-Xlint:unchecked"/> -->
      <classpath refid="astgen.classpath"/>
      <include name="**/*.java"/>
      <exclude name="${usefulPackage}/*.java"/>
      <exclude name="${unicodePackage}/*.java"/>
    </javac>
    <!-- The <scalac> pass that stood here compiled **/*.scala from
         ${astgen.generators.src}, which contains no Scala sources (and the
         task itself is gone from Scala 2.13).  If ASTGen generators ever
         gain Scala sources, compile them the way compileAll does. -->
  </target>

  <target name="checkNodesUptodate" depends="astGenerators">
    <condition property="nodes.uptodate">
      <and>
        <available file="${nodes}/AbstractNode.java"/>
        <uptodate srcfile="${astgen.src}/Fortress.ast"
                  targetfile="${nodes}/AbstractNode.java"/>
        <available file="${library}/FortressAst.fsi" />
        <uptodate srcfile="${astgen.src}/Fortress.ast"
                  targetfile="${library}/FortressAst.fsi" />
        <available file="${library}/FortressAst.fss" />
        <uptodate srcfile="${astgen.src}/Fortress.ast"
                  targetfile="${library}/FortressAst.fss" />
        <uptodate targetfile="${library}/FortressAst.fsi">
          <srcfiles dir="${PF}/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/" includes="**/*.java"/>
        </uptodate>
      </and>
    </condition>
    <echo message="Nodes up to date? ${nodes.uptodate}"/>
  </target>

  <taskdef name="astgen" classpath="${astgen.third}/astgen.jar;${build}"
           classname="edu.rice.cs.astgen.AntTask"/>

  <target name="makeAST" unless="nodes.uptodate" depends="checkNodesUptodate"
          description="Automatically generate AST nodes.">
    <echo message="Processing ${generate-sourcefile}" />
    <astgen file="${generate-sourcefile}" />
    <move todir="${nodes}">
      <fileset dir="${astgen.src}">
        <include name="**/*.java"/>
        <exclude name="**/Fortress.ast"/>
      </fileset>
    </move>
    <replace dir="${nodes}"
             token="java.lang.Object"
             value="Object" />
    <!-- Normalize the generation timestamp that ASTGen's NodeClass (inside
         astgen.jar) stamps into each node's @version javadoc line, so that
         regeneration is byte-identical and the checked-in nodes/ tree does
         not churn on every clean build.  The in-repo generators
         (TemplateGapClass, EllipsesNode, TransformationNode) emit this
         normalized form directly. -->
    <replaceregexp byline="true"
                   match="^( \* @version  Generated automatically by ASTGen) at .*$"
                   replace="\1 from Fortress.ast">
      <fileset dir="${nodes}" includes="**/*.java"/>
    </replaceregexp>
    <!-- Hash each node apart from the JVM's identity hashes, so that hash
         maps and sets of nodes iterate in one order whatever code asked for
         an identity hash before.  ASTGen's NodeClass starts each node's
         hash from the Class object's identity hash: start it from the hash
         of the class's name, which String.hashCode fixes.  The Option
         classes hash by identity hashes too, so a field whose type holds an
         Option is hashed by NodeHash.  The in-repo generators write the
         class name's hash directly, and none of their fields holds an
         Option. -->
    <replaceregexp byline="true"
                   match="^(\s*int code = getClass\(\))\.hashCode\(\);$"
                   replace="\1.getName().hashCode();">
      <fileset dir="${nodes}" includes="**/*.java"/>
    </replaceregexp>
    <replaceregexp flags="g"
                   match="(Option<[^\n]*> (temp_\w+) = [^\n]*;\n\s*code \^= )\2\.hashCode\(\);"
                   replace="\1NodeHash.of(\2);">
      <fileset dir="${nodes}" includes="**/*.java"/>
    </replaceregexp>
    <move todir="${library}">
      <fileset dir="${astgen.src}">

      <exclude name="${unicodePackage}/*.java"/>

          depends="compileCommon, makeAST, parser, operatorsGen">

          <isset property="nodes.uptodate"/>
          <isset property="parser.uptodate"/>
          <isset property="operators.uptodate"/>
        </and>

    <property name="sources.compiled" value="${sources.start}"
              unless:set="sources.regenerated"/>
    <sourcesFingerprint property="sources.compiled" if:set="sources.regenerated"/>
    <condition property="sources.as.built">
      <equals arg1="${sources.compiled}" arg2="${built.sources}"/>
    </condition>
    <implementationFingerprint property="implementation.before"
                               if:set="sources.as.built"/>
    <condition property="scala.uptodate">
      <and>
        <isset property="sources.as.built"/>
        <equals arg1="${implementation.before}" arg2="${built.stamp}"/>
      </and>
    </condition>

          description="Compile the Scala sources (part of compileAll).">

         too, which parses them for signatures but emits classes only for

         .java sources for real.  The file list goes through an @argfile to
         keep the command line short. -->

      <fileset dir="${src}">
        <include name="**/*.java"/>
        <include name="**/*.scala"/>
        <exclude name="${usefulPackage}/*.java"/>
        <exclude name="${unicodePackage}/*.java"/>
      </fileset>
    </pathconvert>
    <pathconvert property="scalac.compileAll.classpath" refid="compile.classpath"/>
    <echo file="${build}/scalac-compileAll.args" message="${scalac.compileAll.sources}"/>
    <java classname="scala.tools.nsc.Main" fork="true" failonerror="true"
          maxmemory="1024m">
      <classpath refid="scala.classpath"/>
      <arg value="-d"/>
      <arg value="${build}"/>
      <arg value="-classpath"/>
      <arg value="${scalac.compileAll.classpath}"/>
      <arg value="-encoding"/>
      <arg value="UTF-8"/>
      <arg value="-deprecation"/>

          description="Compile all Fortress code.">

        target="${javaSourceVersion}"

      <classpath refid="compile.classpath"/>

      <exclude name="${usefulPackage}/*.java"/>
      <exclude name="${unicodePackage}/*.java"/>

    <condition property="build.unchanged">
      <and>
        <isset property="scala.uptodate"/>
        <not><isset property="java.compiled"/></not>
      </and>
    </condition>

              if:set="build.unchanged"/>
    <implementationFingerprint property="implementation.built"
                               unless:set="build.unchanged"/>
